Hector Berlioz. The French Romantic composer, conductor, and critic who made monumental contributions to modern orchestration and program music.

Unlike most composers of his era, Berlioz did not play the piano. Instead, he played the flute and guitar. He was a literary-minded composer, frequently basing works on Shakespeare, Byron, and Virgil.

His most famous work is the Symphonie fantastique from 1830, a radical program symphony depicting an artist's drug-induced hallucinations about his beloved. It is a five-movement masterpiece which depicts an artist poisoning himself with opium out of unrequited love. It features the famous movements March to the Scaffold and Dream of a Witches' Sabbath.

Berlioz coined the term Idée fixe, or Fixed idea, for the recurring melody that represents the beloved woman, which appears in various guises in all five movements of the symphony.

Harriet Smithson was the Irish actress whom Berlioz saw playing Ophelia in Paris. This sparked the obsessive infatuation that inspired the Symphonie fantastique. They later married, though the union was unhappy.

Berlioz wrote a treatise on orchestration called the Grand traité d'instrumentation et d'orchestration modernes, published in 1844. This book codified modern orchestral writing and was later updated by Richard Strauss.

Harold in Italy, Op. 16 is a symphonic work with a prominent solo viola part. It is based on Lord Byron's Childe Harold's Pilgrimage and was commissioned by Niccolò Paganini.

In the witches' sabbath finale, Berlioz famously quotes the Dies irae, the medieval Gregorian chant for the dead. He has it sound in the tubas and bassoons to signify death and damnation.

Berlioz was inspired by Beethoven's Pastoral Symphony to expand the symphonic structure to five movements. He was a pioneer of programmatic French Romanticism who composed several operas, including the massive Les Troyens based on Virgil's Aeneid.
